title: Why the Sky Is Blue
artefact:
The sky looks blue because of how sunlight interacts with the air. Sunlight that looks white is actually a mixture of all the visible colours, each with a different wavelength. Red and orange light have long wavelengths; blue and violet light have short ones.

As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, it strikes molecules of nitrogen and oxygen that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These molecules scatter the light in all directions. The amount of scattering depends sharply on wavelength: it rises roughly as one over the wavelength to the fourth power. This relationship is called Rayleigh scattering. Because the dependence is so steep, short-wavelength blue light is scattered far more strongly than long-wavelength red light, by a factor of around ten.

When you look at the sky away from the Sun, the light reaching your eye has been scattered out of the direct beam, and that scattered light is dominated by the blue end of the spectrum. So the sky appears blue. You might ask why it is not violet, since violet scatters even more. There are two reasons: the Sun emits less violet than blue, and the human eye is less sensitive to violet.

At sunset the light travels a longer path through the atmosphere, so most of the blue is scattered away before it reaches you, leaving the reds and oranges. The same physics that makes the midday sky blue makes the setting Sun red.
